paras: The beating of Sanders at the Atlantic Coast Line shops in Wilmington, North Carolina, was an assault on a Black railroad shop worker by a crowd of his fellow workmen in the spring of 1903, after he was said to have cursed one of them. Sanders was beaten but not seriously hurt, and the Black workers at the shops, numbered at 500, walked off the job in response. The walkout and a company investigation carried the story to papers in North Carolina, Georgia and South Carolina.

According to the Dawson News, Sanders was one of about 500 Black men employed about the Atlantic Coast Line shops at Wilmington to do heavy work. The same account added that it was "rumored that trouble between the two races has been brewing for some time."

Sanders was said to have cursed one of the workmen, whom a Wilmington dispatch to the Raleigh News & Observer described as white. At the noon hour, when the men stopped for dinner, a crowd of the shop workmen set upon him; the Dawson News put their number at "over two hundred" and said they "almost mobbed" him. He was "badly beaten" in the Dawson account and "pretty roughly handled" in the Raleigh one, but both said he suffered no serious injury.

The Black workers responded at once: the Dawson News said the entire force walked out and refused to work the rest of the day, while the Raleigh dispatch said all the Black shop employees "at once struck."

The Coast Line management began an investigation, which the Dawson News said would "probe the matter to the bottom." No report of arrests, of the investigation's findings or of the workers' return appears in the coverage.

Only white papers carried the story, and none of them from Wilmington itself. The Dawson News in Georgia printed the fullest account on April 1 under the headline "Race Trouble in Shops," opening with the cause as it saw it: "Because a negro cursed one of the workmen." The Raleigh News & Observer ran a short special from Wilmington, "A Negro Roughly Handled," on April 4 and again, word for word, on April 5.

Both accounts put the cursing first and the attack second, and both stressed that the injuries were not serious, without comment on the attackers. By April 9 the Bamberg Herald in South Carolina had reduced the episode to a single line in a news digest about 500 Black workers who quit "on account of trouble with the white employees," with no mention of the beating. No Black newspaper account of the episode appears in the coverage.

The accounts differ on the date: the Dawson News, printed April 1, placed the attack on a Thursday, which would be March 26, while the Raleigh dispatch dated April 3 said it happened "yesterday," April 2. Because the Dawson account appeared before April 2, the earlier date is better supported, and the Raleigh dispatch may have been delayed or misdated.

reader.title: Beating of Sanders at the Atlantic Coast Line shops, Wilmington
bases: A crowd of fellow shop workmen beat a Black worker, Sanders, after he was said to have cursed one of them; no killing or threat to kill is reported (A1, A2).

Two separately worded reports, a Wilmington special to the Raleigh News & Observer (A2) and the Dawson News item (A1), agree on the victim's name, the place, the pretext, the beating and the walkout, though they differ on the date and the size of the crowd.

accounts.label: Dawson News report
accounts.gist: Because Sanders cursed a workman on Thursday, over two hundred fellow workmen almost mobbed him at noon and beat him badly but not seriously; the whole Black force of 500 walked out and the Coast Line began an investigation.

accounts.label: Wilmington special to the News & Observer
accounts.gist: Dated April 3: Sanders, who cursed a white workman 'yesterday', was attacked by a crowd at the dinner hour and roughly handled without serious injury; all Black shop employees struck and officials would investigate.

framing.detail: The Dawson News ran it as 'Race Trouble in Shops', giving the cursing as the cause ('Because a negro cursed...') and the beating as a near-mobbing, without comment on the attackers.
The News & Observer's brief 'A Negro Roughly Handled' opened with the cursing and stressed that Sanders 'received no serious injuries'.
The Bamberg Herald reduced it to a one-line item on 500 Black workers quitting over 'trouble with the white employees', omitting the beating.

conflicts.note: The Dawson News printed its account on April 1, before the April 2 date implied by the Raleigh dispatch, so the March 26 date is better supported unless there were two incidents; the Raleigh dispatch may have been delayed or misdated. Not resolved by the coverage.
